clips.text: Rabbits breed. Foxes eat rabbits. When rabbits are plentiful, foxes thrive. Then rabbits get scarce, foxes go hungry, and the rabbits recover. The two populations rise and fall in cycles.
Now imagine many species, their interactions organised by a tree-shaped network. Here are two for four species: a chain and a star. Could they secretly behave exactly the same way? Pause and guess.
The answer is no, apart from rare special cases. And one thing first: someone else announced this result earlier. What you'll see is an independent check of it, not a first discovery.
Start with rabbits alone, growing by about ten percent a month. A hundred become about a hundred and ten, then about a hundred and twenty-two.
The rate of change is the gradient of this graph, written d r by d t. Here it is nought point one times r: growth proportional to the population.
Now add foxes. The more foxes there are, the slower the rabbits grow. The rabbits' rate of change is r, times two minus f.
And foxes need food. Their rate of change is f, times r minus three.
To see the whole story at once, use a plane: rabbits across, foxes up. Each point is a possible state, and its arrow shows where that state is heading.
Follow the arrows and you go round a loop: the cycle. These are the Lotka-Volterra equations, about a century old.

With more species, each follows the same kind of rule: its population, times a weighted sum of all the populations. There are no separate birth or death numbers, so every term is two populations multiplied.
The weights fit in a table. Row one says how species one responds to each species. This four-species table is our running example.
The big negative numbers on the diagonal mean that each species crowds itself out.

Now the network. Draw each species as a dot and join some pairs with lines. With no loops, and every dot reachable from every other, it's a tree. Four dots allow just two trees: the chain and the star.
Careful: the tree is not a food web. In these systems every species can affect every other. Instead, the tree is a rule about which effects must be equal.
Here's the rule. Remove species two, and the chain falls into branches: one on one side, three and four on the other. Species two must affect everything in a branch equally.

In the table, that's column two: a one for species one, and a two for both three and four. Every column follows this rule, leaving ten free numbers instead of sixteen. All such tables form the chain family.
The star gives its own pattern. Removing the centre leaves three branches, so column one has three different numbers.
To picture this, suppose species three and four are absent. They stay absent, since their rate of change is zero times something. So we can watch species one and two on a plane, with arrows.

Now describe the same motion in new variables: mixtures of the old ones. Keep x one, and replace x two by twenty-seven x two minus twenty-six x one. The grid shears, the arrows go with it, but only the description changed.
Usually, the new rules look nothing like our equations. But this time they have the same shape again: each variable, times a weighted sum. Only the table changed.
When mixing turns one system exactly into another, the two are called equivalent: the same system in disguise. So the real question is: can a chain system be disguised as a star system?
In twenty twenty-five, Peter van der Kamp conjectured no, for any two different trees, and checked it up to eight species.
Why did that particular mixture work? Pause and think about it.
Start simple. An absent species stays absent, because its rate of change is itself times something. Anything with that property, once zero, stays zero.
Our mixture, twenty-seven x two minus twenty-six x one, is one of these. Work out its rate of change, and it factorises: the mixture itself, times minus twenty-five x one minus twenty-six x two.
So on the line where the mixture is zero, the motion stays on that line. Start species one and two in the ratio twenty-seven to twenty-six, and they keep that ratio forever.
Quantities like this are called Darboux polynomials: hidden invariants. They aren't conserved themselves, but their zeros are. And our mixing simply turned this hidden line into an axis.
A tree system has one for each species, and one for each tree line, mixing just its two ends; the tree rule makes that work. The chain has four plus three: seven. So does the star.
Here's why they matter. Mixing can't create or destroy a hidden invariant; it just rewrites each one. So equivalent systems have matching sets.
But mixing scrambles the formulas. After this mixing, x three minus x four has become plain y one. You can no longer tell which invariants were single species.

So what survives? Take x one, x two, and twenty-seven x two minus twenty-six x one. The third is built from the other two, and stays so after any mixing. Call three invariants like this a linked triple.
Each tree line gives one linked triple: its two ends and their mixture. Draw each as a triangle. Mixing can move everything around, but it never changes which triples are linked.
Now count. In the chain, two invariants sit in two triangles each. In the star, one sits in three. Mixing can't change that, so a chain system can never be disguised as a star system.
But there's a hole. What if there are hidden invariants we haven't found? Extra ones could form extra triangles and spoil the count.

First, a mixture can't skip a species. Mix species one and three but not two: species two affects one with strength one, but three with strength two, since they're in different branches. That mismatch breaks it.
Next, try three in a row: amounts p one, p two and p three of species one, two and three. Writing out the condition gives one equation per pair, with numbers from the table.
Take the first equation, subtract twenty-six times the second, and add the third. The p two terms cancel. The p three terms cancel. What's left is fifty-five p one equals zero.
But p one isn't zero: species one is in the mixture. Contradiction. Bigger mixtures contain three in a row, so they fail too. The only hidden invariants are single species and the tree's pairs.
That fifty-five comes from column two: one plus twenty-six, plus two plus twenty-six. The proof needs sums like this to be non-zero. Generic means ruling out such rare coincidences.
This cancellation, with letters in place of numbers, was checked line by line in Lean, a program that verifies proofs.
An invariant in two or more triangles is a species with several neighbours. A triangle joining two of those is a line between them; a triangle with one adds an end species.
Here it is on a seven-species tree, starting from triangles alone. The rule rebuilds the tree exactly, for any size. So generic systems from different trees are never equivalent.
Now the history. These tree families were introduced in twenty twenty-three by Quispel, Tapley, McLaren and van der Kamp. The conjecture followed in twenty twenty-five.

In September twenty twenty-six, a preprint by Zijian Zeng announced this result. It has since been withdrawn and its text is unavailable, so the arguments can't be compared. Withdrawal doesn't erase the announcement.
This work gives an independent, self-contained proof of a closely matching theorem. It is a verification note, not a first discovery, and it claims no priority.

The written proof covers every size. Exact computer checks passed for all nine hundred and eighty-six trees up to twelve species and, at chosen numbers, the full invariant lists for two hundred trees up to ten. Consistency checks, not a proof.
Lean checks only the three-in-a-row step. The rest is a written proof, reviewed internally, but not yet by outside referees.
There are limits. Special tables are excluded: if every row is the same, every mixture is an invariant and the tree is lost. And the tree is a rule about equal effects, not a food web read from data.

To recap. One: each tree defines a family of population systems. Two: their hidden invariants form linked triples, one per tree line, and mixing can't change how they overlap. Three: the overlaps rebuild the tree, so different trees give genuinely different systems.
Still open: what exactly happens at the special tables, where extra invariants appear? And which networks beyond trees can be recovered this way?
